summary: Software that works is not necessarily well designed. Rotting design shows 3 symptoms: Rigidity, Fragility, Immobility.
The OO design goal is to MINIMISE THE IMPACT OF CHANGE, mainly by managing dependencies between classes and packages.
Design for change with encapsulation, low (loose) coupling and high cohesion, keeping reuse, extensibility and maintainability in mind.
Prefer delegation (has-a) over inheritance when you only want to reuse code, and model roles as data, not as subclasses.
SOLID per the slides: SRP, OCP (Meyer), LSP (Liskov 1988), ISP, DIP = 'Dependency Injection Principle', also called Inversion of Control.
Frameworks call your code (IoC). Design patterns (Gang of Four) are proven solutions to known problems.
mustMemorise: 3 symptoms of rotting design: Rigidity (hard to change, changes cascade), Fragility (breaks in unrelated places), Immobility (can't reuse, too much baggage)
Objective of OO design: MINIMISE IMPACT OF CHANGE, by managing dependencies
Class design guidelines: design with Reuse, Extensibility, Maintainability in mind, to achieve Loose (Low) Coupling and High Cohesion
Designing for change: Encapsulation, Low Coupling, High Cohesion
SRP = cohesion: 'never more than ONE reason for a class to change'. Avoid God classes
OCP: 'open for extension, closed for modification'. Originated with Bertrand Meyer. Abstraction is the key
LSP: Barbara Liskov, 1988. Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types
LSP as a contract: preconditions NO STRONGER (expect no more), postconditions NO WEAKER (provide no less)
ISP: 'Many client-specific interfaces are better than one general-purpose interface'. Avoid FAT interfaces

DIP (the slides call it the Dependency INJECTION Principle): high-level modules must not depend on low-level ones, both depend on abstractions; abstractions must not depend on details. Also called IoC, at the heart of framework design
Gang of Four: Gamma, Helm, Johnson, Vlissides. Examples: Singleton, Adapter, Observer, and MVC (for the web)

items.title: Working is not the same as good design
notes: Software can work right now and still be badly designed, showing symptoms that it will break later.
A likely true/false statement.

items.title: Symptoms of rotting design: exactly 3
notes: **Rigidity**: hard to change, even in simple ways. Every change *cascades* into dependent modules.
**Fragility**: breaks in many places on each change, often in areas with *no conceptual relationship* to the change.
**Immobility**: cannot *reuse* the module in other projects or parts, because it depends on too much baggage.
Only these 3 are on the slides. 'Viscosity' comes from Martin's paper and is not on the slide list.

items.title: Match the picture to the symptom
notes: Dominoes / ripple / snowball (change cascades) = **Rigidity**.
Slide 8, tangled cables ('try unplug a cable?') = **Immobility**: you can't pull one part out to reuse it.
Slide 9, junk heap / messy wardrobe = **Fragility**.
Trap: 'breaks somewhere unrelated' is Fragility, not Rigidity. 'Every change forces more changes' is Rigidity.

items.title: Kernighan and Plauger quote
notes: Good design is learned by studying and imitating good programs, not from generalities.
The authors are Kernighan and Plauger, of *The Elements of Programming Style*. The slide writes 'Styles', but the real title is singular.
The long chain in red, `order.getCustomers(..).iterator().next().getName()...`, couples you to many classes and is hard to maintain. The slide gives no explanation, so this reading is inferred.

items.title: OO design goals
notes: Make software **easier to change** when we want to.
A class may change because we want to (new function, business rules) or because something it **depends on** changed (e.g. a method signature).
**Manage dependencies** to minimise the impact of change, and minimise the reasons a module is *forced* to change.

items.title: Objective: MINIMISE IMPACT OF CHANGE
notes: Much of OO design is about **managing dependencies**. You can hardly write OO code without some dependency.
If asked for 'the objective of OO design goals', answer: minimise impact of change.

items.title: Class design guidelines
notes: Manage coupling and cohesion by designing with **Reuse**, **Extensibility** and **Maintainability** in mind.
The aim: **Loose (Low) Coupling and High Cohesion**.
Trap: 'high coupling' or 'low cohesion' in an option is always the bad answer.

items.title: Designing for change: Encapsulation, Low Coupling, High Cohesion
notes: A modular program has well-defined, simple, **independent** units that interact through well-defined **interfaces**.
'Tight' is crossed out and replaced by **Loose**. Class design is not network design: avoid the everything-connected-to-everything mesh.
Low cohesion = an object 'not sure what it does' (the man holding every tool). Cohesive objects 'do one thing, and only one thing, well'.
Slide 15: encapsulation means data and helpers are private and the public methods form the interface.

items.title: Data persistence (bad): DataManager validates everything
notes: Bad encapsulation: DataManager must know the inner workings of Customer and Account (how passwords are stored and compared).
Code typo: `passwd().equals(pwd)` calls a method `passwd()`, but `passwd` is a String variable. Real Java: compile error (cannot find symbol). It should be `passwd.equals(pwd)`.
Exam: treat the code as pseudocode. The point is the bad encapsulation.

items.title: Data persistence (better): each entity validates itself
notes: Better encapsulation: Customer and Account are responsible for their own validation and persistence. DataManager just *manages* the entities (dashed arrows to them = dependency).
Hashing could be added inside `Customer.validate` without touching DataManager.
Code typos: `new Customer(cusID)` is missing `;`, and `c.validate(String pwd)` puts a type inside a call. It should be `c.validate(pwd)`. Pseudocode only.

items.title: Finance index (bad): 3 named problems
notes: **Tight coupling**: NASDAQ and DataDisplay need each other to work.
**Low cohesion**: NASDAQ both tracks data *and* manages the display.
**Bad encapsulation**: NASDAQ must know DataDisplay's inner workings (the `displayType`).
Learn which description goes with which term. MCQs often swap them.

items.title: Finance index (better)
notes: `displayType` moves into DataDisplay. NASDAQ only holds data and `getData()`, giving high cohesion.
The solid line with an open arrowhead from DataDisplay to NASDAQ is a one-way (navigable) association: DataDisplay knows NASDAQ, NASDAQ doesn't know DataDisplay.
DataDisplay `notify()` pulls the data and decides how to display it (an Observer-like idea). The code `display(NASDAQ.getData()` is pseudocode with a missing `)`.

items.title: Bank account: interact via interfaces
notes: `<<interface>>` Account and AccountInfoDisplay. A dashed line with a hollow triangle is **realisation** (`implements`): SavingsAccount, CheckingAccount; ATM/Web/PhoneDisplay.
Client - - -> `<<use>>` is a **dependency**.
On slide 23, adding phone output meant editing the class (`formatForPhone`). Here you just add PhoneDisplay, the OCP idea. 'Interaction via interfaces promotes loose coupling.'

items.title: Inheritance (is-a) vs delegation (has-a)
notes: Left: abstract `Graph {abstract}` with `# plotData() {abstract}` (protected abstract) and `+ draw()`. ScatterPlot and BarChart **extend** it (solid line with hollow triangle) and override `# plotData()`.
Right: ScatterPlot and BarChart each **have an** `Axes` (navigable association), which the slide calls 'Object Composition'.
Trap: here 'object composition' means has-a / delegation in general. The arrows are plain association arrows, *not* the UML filled-diamond composition notation.

items.title: Inheritance vs delegation: the recompile claim
notes: Slide: with `extends Graph`, BarChart must be recompiled when Graph changes. With `private Axes myAxes;` (delegation) it does not need recompiling when Axes changes.
This is a simplification: if Axes's public methods that BarChart uses change, BarChart still needs recompiling. The real point is that delegation means **looser coupling** than inheritance.
Exam: answer as the slide says (delegation leads to less impact of change).

items.title: Inheritance vs role
notes: Lecturer and Student as subclasses of Person: OK on the slide.
Father and Mother as subclasses of Person: crossed out (X). These are **roles** a person plays, and a person can hold several or change them.
Model a role as data instead: `Person father = new Person();` plus an `enum FAMILY_ROLE {...}`.

items.title: SOLID, and the D is named 'Injection' here
notes: S = Single Responsibility, O = Open-Closed, L = Liskov Substitution, I = Interface Segregation, **D = Dependency Injection Principle (DIP)** per these slides.
The standard name (Robert C. Martin) is the Dependency **Inversion** Principle. The slides say 'Injection'.
Exam: if the question uses the slide wording, answer 'Dependency Injection Principle'. If only 'Inversion' is offered, it is the same principle.

items.title: SRP
notes: Quote: "There should never be more than ONE reason for a class to change".
SRP **= cohesion**. Each responsibility is an *axis of change*.
More than one responsibility gives more than one reason to change, and the responsibilities become coupled. Avoid a 'God' class.
The picture shows a judge and a doctor: separate roles, separate classes.

items.title: OCP: Bertrand Meyer
notes: "A module should be **open for extension** but **closed for modification**".
OCP **originated from Bertrand Meyer** (not Liskov, not Martin).
Change what a module does *without changing its source code*. **Abstraction is the key** to OCP.

items.title: OCP example: Transport fares
notes: Bad (top): one Transport class with `-type` and `calFare()` holding a `switch(type)` over BUS/TAXI/MRT. A new transport (tricycle) means editing that switch.
Good (green box): abstract Transport (padlock = closed), with Bus, Taxi and MRT subclasses (hollow triangle) each overriding `+calFare(): double`.
Adding Tricycle = a new subclass, and Transport and Client stay unchanged. Client - - -> Transport is a dependency.

items.title: LSP: Barbara Liskov, 1988
notes: Formal: if for each o1 of type S there is an o2 of type T such that every program P defined in terms of T behaves *unchanged* when o1 is substituted for o2, then **S is a subtype of T**.
**Barbara Liskov first wrote in 1988** (per slide).
Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types. A **user** of the base class must still work properly when given a derived object.
Slides 34 and 35 animate 'User - - -> Sub1 / Sub2': the user wrote code against Base but receives a subclass.

items.title: LSP as design by contract
notes: Methods state **preconditions** (true before) and **postconditions** (true after).
A subclass is substitutable if its preconditions are **no stronger** (*expect no more*) and its postconditions are **no weaker** (*provide no less*).
Trap: options that swap these ('preconditions no weaker', 'postconditions no stronger') are wrong.
The slide labels both conditions 'a)'. It is a typo for a) and b).

items.title: Noodle analogy
notes: The price rising from $3 to $4 ('I need more!!') = a subtype that **expects more**: a stronger precondition, so it violates LSP.
The fishball crossed out = a subtype that **provides less**: a weaker postcondition, so it violates LSP.
Slide 37's sad face = the user breaks because Sub1 demands more.

items.title: LSP violation: ATMDisplay
notes: The base `format(acc)` handles `null` itself and returns the **full** view.
`ATMDisplay` *assumes the client checks for null*: **expects more**, so it violates LSP. It returns **partial** details: **provides less**, also a violation.
Key point: it compiles and ATMDisplay is-a AccountInfoDisplay, but the **behaviour** breaks the user. Compiling or passing an is-a check does not mean LSP holds.
Code bug: `if (acc == null) return ;` in a method returning `View` is a compile error ('missing return value'). Read it as `return null;`.

items.title: Classic LSP violation: Square extends Rectangle
notes: Square overrides both setters to keep width == height.
`r.setWidth(5); r.setHeight(10);` on a Square leaves it 10x10, so `getArea()` prints **100**, not the 50 the client expects (verified in JDK 17).
Mathematically a square is-a rectangle, but behaviourally Square cannot substitute for Rectangle, so LSP is violated. Circle/Ellipse is the same story.
The slide's code isn't real Java: `setWidth(w : int)` is UML syntax, and Square writes Rectangle's *private* fields. The output logic is still correct.

items.title: LSP duck poster
notes: "If it looks like a duck, quacks like a duck, but needs batteries, you probably have the wrong abstraction."
Looking like the base type (is-a, same methods) is not enough. Behaviour must match.

items.title: ISP
notes: "**Many client-specific** interfaces are better than **one general-purpose** interface".
Classes should not depend on interfaces they do not use. Avoid **FAT interfaces**.
Picture: a universal plug adapter (one fat thing that tries to fit everything).

items.title: ISP example: fat IAnimal
notes: `IAnimal {fly(); run(); swim();}` forces Tiger to write empty `fly{}` and `swim{}`. Only `run` has real code.
The fix splits it into `IFlyable`, `IRunnable`, `ISwimmable`. The arrows from IAnimal to these just show the split. They are not real UML.
Code bug: `public void fly { }` has no `()`, which is a compile error in real Java (verified).

items.title: ISP result
notes: A dashed line with a hollow triangle is **realisation**: each class implements only what it needs.
Goose implements IFlyable, IRunnable and ISwimmable. Tiger implements IRunnable. Dolphin implements ISwimmable. Crocodile implements IRunnable and ISwimmable.
A Java class can implement many interfaces.

items.title: DIP: the two rules
notes: A. High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. **Both depend on abstractions.**
B. Abstractions should not depend on details. **Details depend on abstractions.**
Then high-level modules can be reused easily. DIP is at the heart of **framework** design.
**Also known as Inversion of Control (IoC).**

items.title: DIP example approach
notes: The demo uses **Reflection** classes, a **mini framework**, and code that plugs into the framework through an **interface or abstract class**.
The cat seeing a lion: what matters is the abstraction you depend on.

items.title: DIP demo: DiscPlayer
notes: DiscPlayer —play→ **Disc** (navigable association to the *abstraction*). DVDDisc and BlurayDisc extend Disc (solid hollow triangle).
DiscPlayerApp has dependencies (dashed open arrows) on DiscPlayer, Disc and ObjectCreator. `ObjectCreator.create()` is **underlined = static**.
The 'VCD' box is a UML **note** (folded corner, dashed link). A new VCD disc type can be added without changing DiscPlayer, because the high-level module depends on the abstraction.

items.title: What a framework is
notes: A large body of prewritten classes. You add your own class that **extends or realises** a framework class or interface.
**The framework is in control and instantiates your class.** You use it by calling its methods and supplying **callbacks**, which is IoC.
Diagram: MyClass extends the italic (abstract) SomeClass inside a package (tabbed folder).

items.title: Design patterns: Gang of Four
notes: GoF = **Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson, John Vlissides**.
A pattern = a **proven solution to a known problem**.
Examples: **Singleton, Adapter, Observer**. **MVC** is a widely used pattern for the web.
